Science.title: New calculations reveal hidden pathways that let chemical reactions produce different products
Science.summary: Chemical reactions are often understood as molecules crossing a high-energy saddle point, known as a transition state, before following a downhill pathway toward a product. Conventional quantum chemical calculations typically trace this single pathway to determine how a reaction proceeds.

Science.title: SpaceX fires up Starship upper stage ahead of landmark Flight 15 test launch (video)
Science.summary: SpaceX just fired up all six engines on the Starship upper stage that will conduct the vehicle's 15th test flight, potentially keeping everything on track for a launch next month.

Science.title: Simplified ancestral enzyme makes ATP without amino acid needed for its usual reaction
Science.summary: Proteins perform essential functions in living organisms, from catalyzing biochemical reactions to supporting cellular energy metabolism. Their functions depend on their amino acid composition and three-dimensional structures. However, early proteins may have evolved when fewer amino acid types were available than those used by most modern proteins.

Science.title: Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy
Science.summary: Mathematicians have uncovered what they argue is a fundamental flaw in the standard model of the universe, potentially challenging the need for dark energy. Their calculations suggest that the mathematical framework used to describe cosmic expansion is inherently unstable and that the universe could accelerate naturally under Einstein's original theory of gravity. The findings also raise surprising questions about whether our location in the universe is as ordinary as scientists have long assumed.

Science.title: Nature finance needs a fundamental rethink, researchers argue
Science.summary: The authors call on governments, investors and conservation organizers to reimagine nature finance based on a central tenet: raising funds should be a means to an end, not an end in itself.

Science.title: Big cats, unexplained lights and a floodlit eclipse — 7 skywatching 'horror stories' to keep you entertained this Halloween
Science.summary: Stargazing doesn't always go to plan, and we have the stories to prove it.

Science.title: Evolutionary changes in key enzyme may help bacteria make proteins faster
Science.summary: Evolutionary changes in a key protein synthesis enzyme, isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase (IleRS), may help bacteria fine-tune how quickly proteins are made, report researchers from Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan; the University of Zagreb Faculty of Science, Croatia; and ETH Zürich, Switzerland.

Science.title: 'This is so crazy!' Virginia college student looking for shark teeth finds rare Native American spearpoint
Science.summary: A biology student found a Native American stone spearpoint when searching for shark teeth along the coast of Virginia.

Science.title: ISS astronaut will conduct Canada's 1st spacewalk in 7 years on Oct. 29: Watch it live
Science.summary: Joshua Kutryk will venture outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, on the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in more than seven years. Here's how to watch it live.

Science.title: A 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals a lost world where early humans lived
Science.summary: A remarkably preserved elephant tooth dating back nearly 700,000 years has revealed a surprisingly lush prehistoric world where giant elephants and early humans lived side by side. Discovered in northern Israel alongside ancient stone tools, the tooth belonged to a straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Ice Age.

Science.title: How ancient insect-eating diets could inspire more sustainable food systems
Science.summary: New research from Durham University highlights how insects have been part of human diets for thousands of years despite seeming unusual to many people.

Science.title: Ghostly Cat’s Head Nebula Lurks Within Sight of NASA’s Hubble, Webb
Science.summary: Like a spectral form rising out of a cold mist, NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have captured a hauntingly dynamic star-forming scene. It lies within the vast Carina Nebula, a diffuse star-forming region located about 7,500 light-years away from Earth. The small, select area both telescopes observed is nicknamed the Cat’s Head Nebula […]

Science.title: NASA Names Troy Asher Armstrong Flight Research Center Director
Science.summary: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Troy Asher director of the agency’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. Asher, a veteran test pilot and aerospace engineer with decades of experience in flight research and operations, has served as the center’s acting director since March. “Troy has spent his career pushing the boundaries of flight, […]

Science.title: Chemical recycling turns silicone waste into reusable building blocks with up to 99% yield
Science.summary: Silicones are widely used in industry, medicine and everyday products due to their exceptional thermal and chemical stability. However, it is precisely these properties that have made recycling silicones extremely problematic in the past. Researchers at the Institute of Chemistry at TU Berlin have now succeeded in breaking down the polymer chains of silicone molecules into their basic building blocks. The resulting molecule dimethyldichlorosilane can then be reused as a starting material for the production of new silicone compounds.

Science.title: Detailed images reveal ribosome assembly inside human cells for the first time
Science.summary: For decades, ribosomes have been under the lens of many scientists. Ribosomes are highly sophisticated and complex molecular machines that allow cells to synthesize proteins. However, putting ribosomes together requires intricate assembly processes. While many underlying mechanisms for building ribosomes have been discovered ex situ (outside their native cellular context), our understanding of how ribosomes are assembled in situ has so far remained limited.

Science.title: Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
Science.summary: Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. The finding reveals a hidden source of cardiovascular risk and could open the door to new treatments that protect the heart and brain.

Science.title: Waves alter Antarctic polynyas by breaking up surrounding sea ice
Science.summary: Polynyas are one of Antarctica's great counterintuitive features: recurring areas of open water surrounded by vast expanses of sea ice. These unusual environments are hot spots for sea-ice production, ocean–atmosphere exchange and biological productivity. They are commonly maintained by powerful winds that push newly formed ice away from the coast, repeatedly exposing the ocean to the freezing Antarctic atmosphere.

Science.title: Send Your Name to Titan Aboard NASA’s Dragonfly Mission
Science.summary: You may never soar under the clouds or over the organic sands of Saturn’s moon Titan, but your name can. Science.title: Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered that magma deep inside Earth can store surprising amounts of extra oxygen, potentially revealing a hidden contributor to our planet's oxygen-rich atmosphere. The findings suggest that ancient volcanic eruptions may have helped transform Earth's atmosphere billions of years ago, with implications for understanding life on other planets.

Science.title: Qinghai–Tibet Plateau study traces evolution of terrestrial animals across three distinct regions
Science.summary: A new study has pieced together the evolutionary history of terrestrial animals on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (QTP), offering a comprehensive picture of how the distinctive fauna of the "Third Pole" took shape over millions of years.

Science.title: How eggs protect chromosome connections during prolonged dormancy
Science.summary: Eggs follow a very different developmental path from sperm. Once a male hits puberty, sperm cells are produced continuously throughout his life. Eggs, however, are all produced during the fetal stage. Once formed, eggs enter a long dormant state called the dictyate stage, in which the process of cell division (meiosis) is paused partway through. This dormant period ends only when the egg is ovulated.

Science.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
Science.summary: When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one […]

Science.title: Meteors don't just burn up. What really happens is far more violent
Science.summary: Scientists have uncovered seven surprising stages that space rocks go through as they hurtle toward Earth, revealing that melting and violent fragmentation, rather than simple evaporation, determine their fate. The discovery could help explain why meteorites scatter across the ground and how dangerous asteroids explode in Earth's atmosphere.

Science.title: NASA’s Hubble Marks Way for Roman Space Telescope
Science.summary: A sweeping barred galaxy takes center stage in this Oct. 22, 2026, image, but the gravitational lensing at bottom right is the real target. This observation is one of many gravitational lensing images taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope in preparation for science with the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Astronomers will use these […]

Science.title: NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s
Science.summary: NASA’s Juno spacecraft has discovered that Jupiter uses a surprisingly complex system of powerful plasma waves and multiple shock regions to defend against the solar wind. The findings reveal major differences between Jupiter and Earth and could help scientists understand the enormous shock waves produced by exploding stars.

Science.title: Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman named deputy director for NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
Science.summary: The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty.

Science.title: What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery
Science.summary: The penguins that perished lived on the Danger Islands in Antarctica. The prime suspect was avian flu. Researchers were surprised by what they found.

Science.title: A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
Science.summary: Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments.

Science.title: Faraway tectonic forces may have accelerated the Gulf of California rifting
Science.summary: When the Baja California peninsula broke from mainland Mexico nearly 12 million years ago, it gave rise to the Gulf of California. New research suggests that this process of continental rifting was greatly accelerated due to tectonic forces on the opposite side of the Pacific Ocean.

Science.summary: When companies began approaching NASA’s Langley Research Center, asking to be included in the In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing (ISAM) State of Play for access to competitive intelligence, the team knew they had crossed an inflection point. “We’ve had some unnamed companies ask if we have any proprietary information,” says Dale Arney, senior team lead […]

Science.title: Researchers observe the arrival of El Niño in Monterey Bay
Science.summary: For more than 30 years, MBARI technology has recorded real-time data about Monterey Bay, from oceanographic conditions at the surface to biological surveys in the depths of Monterey Canyon. These data are integral to understanding our changing ocean and underpin the institute's efforts to monitor the impacts of the incoming El Niño, which has been predicted to be among the strongest since the beginning of modern oceanography.

Science.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
Science.summary: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.

Science.title: Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
Science.summary: Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.

Science.title: New simulation shows the first 2 billion years of the universe's history play out in stunning detail
Science.summary: A new program aims to help scientists figure out how the ingredients of the universe formed early galaxies, which lit up the cosmos after a "dark age."

Science.title: Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics
Science.summary: Scientists have defied a long-standing rule of laser physics by generating X-rays with much higher energies than conventional theory predicts. The surprising discovery reveals how two electrons working together can overcome a previously accepted limit, opening new possibilities for quantum research.

Science.title: Wild orchids face growing challenges as conservation falls short
Science.summary: At first glance, it is easy to see why Corybas puniceus has captured the attention of collectors around the world. Small enough to fit in the palm of your hand, its unusual shape and bursts of color make it unlike almost anything else in the orchid world. The species, found only in Southeast Asia, is classified as critically endangered.

Science.title: Keeping one eye open: Veterinarian applies unique treatment to preserve dog's eyesight
Science.summary: Aparna Shah teaches Virginia Tech students how the human eye turns light into sight. In May, she saw her dog lose his.

Science.title: Terahertz light distinguishes two groups of particles trapped inside superconducting vortices
Science.summary: Scientists at Rutgers and in Estonia have used invisible light to look into tiny magnetic whirlpools, called vortices, inside a superconductor, revealing details that could help researchers develop better materials for carrying electricity.

Science.title: The 'shape' of gene expression: Identifying genes that may share roles across species
Science.summary: Much of what we know about biology comes from animal models, particularly mice. Applying these insights to humans, however, is not always straightforward. For example, some of the genes important for the formation of germ cells, which eventually give rise to eggs or sperm, differ between mice and humans.

Science.title: Bright object beyond Pluto may be the solar system's sixth dwarf planet
Science.summary: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a new dwarf planet in our solar system, orbiting the sun on an inclined plane past Pluto.

Science.title: Bronze Age sword discovered in an Italian lake is still sharp after 3,300 years
Science.summary: Archaeologists found several ancient weapons, intact vases and a bronze razor in the volcanic crater lake.

Science.title: European rivers retain far more plastic than they carry to the sea, study finds
Science.summary: Plastic that enters the environment does not necessarily make its way to the sea via rivers. In fact, only a tiny fraction eventually reaches river mouths. Most plastic remains on land or within river systems.

Science.title: Using machine learning to build safer cities
Science.summary: In eThekwini, researchers have harnessed machine learning and satellite data to spot the city's most landslide-prone zones. A new study published in Scientific Reports has found that urban development activities, including road construction, property development and vegetation loss, are significantly increasing landslide susceptibility across parts of eThekwini.

Science.title: What animal bones in Malawi teach us about the social lives of people long ago
Science.summary: In the ancient past, when human communities were small and the only way to travel was by walking, what were the chances of meeting a stranger? And what would happen next?

Science.title: Stunning solar eclipse photos reveal giant hole and mysterious 'smoke rings' in the sun's atmosphere
Science.summary: Solar eclipse photography provides a unique vista into the processes taking place in the sun's upper atmosphere.

Science.title: Study reveals new clues to why colorectal cancer in young people is so deadly
Science.summary: Colorectal cancer in young people shows genetic and structural differences that may make it more aggressive and treatment-resistant than the cancer tends to be in older people.

Science.title: Sex after baby: How childhood trauma can get in the way
Science.summary: Why do some parents have more sexual difficulties than others after having a baby? Childhood trauma plays a significant role, amplifying the other factors at play.

Science.title: Measuring multiple reactions on a single electrode with extraordinary sensitivity
Science.summary: A reaction on a single electrode can tell scientists a remarkable amount about the chemical nature and number of analytes involved. The challenge comes when they want to distinguish many reactions on the same electrode. After more than a decade of trying to overcome that limitation, Ravi Saraf and his Nebraska Engineering graduate students have demonstrated a way to quantify many reactions on the same electrode without sacrificing extraordinary sensitivity.

Science.title: 'Crystal Lake' is great, but nothing tops the space horror shenanigans of 'Jason X'
Science.summary: The Voorhees legend continues in Crystal Lake, but Jason X remains the Citizen Kane of this franchise.

Science.title: Even stupendous black holes can’t explain dark matter
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03386-4 The theoretical objects would have left a larger imprint on cosmic radiation if they were a source of the invisible force pulling together the galaxies.

Science.title: How the quantum vacuum perturbs atoms, could shrink black holes and may have helped form galaxies
Science.summary: The word "vacuum" may conjure the image of empty space. Maybe you think of a region far outside the solar system without planets, debris, gas clouds or light. According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty. Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle—which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time—to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still.

Science.title: Eyewitnesses remember feedback better after making an identification, study finds
Science.summary: An eyewitness can tell the truth, believe every word they say and still send an innocent person to prison. A new study by Stephen Charman from FIU's Department of Psychology takes on a question that has challenged the justice system for decades: Can we rely on eyewitnesses to help identify the person responsible for a crime?

Science.title: Decapitated man buried near fort in Roman-era Scotland gets a new virtual face
Science.summary: See the new facial reconstruction of a man from Roman-era Scotland who was decapitated after his death and buried near a Roman fort.

Science.title: Cosmic graveyard of zombie planets offers a grisly warning about our own solar system's fate
Science.summary: Two zombie exoplanets that rose from the grave to shuffle through the gory remains of their fellow planets may just agree with these immortal words from horror maestro Stephen King.

Science.title: Neanderthal DNA still survives in our human family tree. What were our ancient relatives' relationships like?
Science.summary: Developing research suggests that ancient interbreeding wasn't random — it was socially patterned, directional and far more complicated than the headlines suggest.
